John Preston
JON PRES-tun
proper noun
English surname Preston, from Old English prēost-tūn, “priest’s settlement”; the given name John from Hebrew Yochanan, “the LORD is gracious.”

See also: John Preston

📖 Biblical Definition

John Preston, master of Emmanuel College in Cambridge — that seminary of Puritanism — and one of the most influential preachers of his generation, was a man of rare gifts who might have risen to any height at court, yet gave himself wholly to the cause of the gospel and the training of a godly ministry. Converted under the preaching of John Cotton, and standing in that golden chain of Cambridge divines that reached back through Sibbes and Baynes to Perkins, he became a physician of souls whose sermons drew multitudes and whose influence reached even into the councils of state. His posthumous works — among them The Breastplate of Faith and Love, The New Covenant, and The Saints Qualification — are treasuries of covenant divinity and experimental religion, unfolding the freeness of grace, the nature of saving faith, and the everlasting covenant that God makes with His people in Christ. He preached faith and love as the very breastplate by which the Christian is guarded, tracing the marks of the one and the fruits of the other. Cut off in the midst of his usefulness, dying while still a young man, he committed his soul to the covenant God he had preached, and left the church a body of writing by which he, being dead, yet speaketh, teaching the assurance of faith and the sweetness of union with Christ.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Influential master of Emmanuel College, Cambridge, and covenant divine, author of The Breastplate of Faith and Love.

expand to see more

John Preston (1587–1628), master of Emmanuel College, Cambridge, and eminent Puritan preacher.

Converted under John Cotton; heir to the Perkins–Baynes–Sibbes chain of divines.

Author of The Breastplate of Faith and Love, The New Covenant, and other works.

A preacher of covenant divinity whose influence reached into the councils of state.

Died young, in the assurance of the covenant of grace he had proclaimed.

📖 Key Scripture

1Th 5:8 — "But let us, who are of the day, be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love; and for an helmet, the hope of salvation."

Gen 17:7 — "And I will establish my covenant between me and thee and thy seed after thee in their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God unto thee, and to thy seed after thee."

Heb 11:13 — "These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth."

Gal 2:20 — "I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his works recover covenant grace and the assurance of saving faith.

expand to see more

Preston’s memory faces no revisionist campaign, yet the covenant divinity he preached — the free grace of God pledged in an everlasting covenant, laid hold of by a faith that works by love — is little understood in an age that has largely lost the very grammar of covenant. Where Preston set forth God binding Himself by promise to be a God to His people, the modern spirit conceives of religion as a private and contractless sentiment.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the covenant of grace and the assurance it affords — that God has established an everlasting covenant in Christ, that saving faith rests upon His pledged word, and that the believer may put on faith and love as a breastplate against every assault. Preston’s works recover the sweetness of gospel assurance grounded not in the changeable self but in the unchanging promise of the covenant-keeping God.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Rooted in the Reformed doctrine of the covenant of grace and the assurance of saving faith.

The golden chain of Cambridge divines from Perkins to Preston.

Assurance grounded in God’s unchanging promise, not the believer’s frames.
